newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - UK leaps convergence hurdles but shuns EMU.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UK leaps convergence hurdles but shuns EMU.

text.p: Entry to a single European currency would pose few problems for Britain with its glowing set of economic credentials and a new Europe-friendly government, but the country is set to shun the first wave scheduled for January 1999, two Reuters polls published on Wednesday suggested.
Not one of the 49 respondents in Reuters monthly poll on the chance of European economic and monetary union (EMU) starting promptly in 1999 expected Britain to join the first wave.
Asked to give a percentage probability, EMU commentators surveyed across Europe between May 7 and 12 put Britain's chances of first wave membership at an average of just 20 percent.

"History has proved that there is a lot of resistance in the UK. It's too fast a change and they need to consult the electorate," said Gerlof de Vrij, senior bond strategist at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett in Amsterdam.
"Participation from the beginning remains highly unlikely," said Juergen Pfister, head of economic research at Commerzbank in Frankfurt.

But many experts believe Britain's journey towards European integration, which was hesitant under the previous Conservative administration, will now accelerate under the stewardship of the Labour government elected earlier this month.

"It is unlikely to change the timetable up to 1999. However, if EMU proves to be a success, the chances of entry relatively soon after, say 2001, have increased significantly," said Hans Honig, senior economist at Rabobank International in Amsterdam.

Of all EMU contenders, Britain was best placed economically to join EMU after Luxembourg and Finland, according to economists' forecasts for entry criteria highlighted in a second Reuters EMU poll issued on Wednesday.
Average forecasts showed Britain was expected to meet four of the main economic convergence criteria set out in the Maastricht Treaty.
The average forecast of 24 predictions for Britain's debt-to-gross domestic product (GDP) ratio, 56 percent by the end of 1997, was well within the 60 percent laid down by the Maastricht Treaty.

Britain was also seen meeting the budget deficit-to-GDP criterion, albeit by the skin of its teeth. The average predicted level for 1997 was three percent, bang in line with the convergence criteria target. Twenty-four economists submitted forecasts for Britain's predicted deficit-to-GDP ratio.
And despite predictions of higher inflation and long-term interest rates than all other European countries bar Greece in the survey, Britain's score was still within the specified bands.

Inflation should be within 1.5 percent of the average of the three lowest inflation rate countries, the treaty says. The survey results predicted these would be Finland and Sweden and France with an average inflation rate of 1.4 percent.
Long-term interest rates should be within 200 basis points of the average interest rates of the same three countries, which in this survey was 6.38 percent.

With new Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown giving the Bank of England operational responsibility for setting interest rates and the government promising to adopt the European social chapter, Britain seems to be warming to a single currency.

"Labour does look more pro-Europe. An independent Bank of England is the first stop, a referendum could be prepared, and the UK could be ready to join within two years," said Alfredo Urrutia, chief economist at Societe Generale in Madrid.

One possible stumbling block if Britain were to push for prompt entry would be membership of the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM). Britain, along with Sweden and Greece, is outside the ERM, but whether membership is mandatory for entry to the single currency club remains open to question.

Britain's Brown on Monday said he had no plans to take sterling back into ERM, adding that he did not believe the need for ERM membership for two years before being allowed to join EMU was cast in stone.

Analysts agreed the greatest obstacle would be to get the go-ahead from the British public in a referendum. The Labour government has said it will let the people have the final say if parliament decides to join a single currency.
"The public in Britain are not willing to join EMU. Nevertheless, there is a chance that Labour could flirt with joining EMU by 2001," said Marion Swoboda, economist at Credit Suisse in Zurich.
